title: Mars Tracker
narrative: Where things stand on 10 November 2026. Two NASA rovers are working on the surface: Curiosity and Perseverance. Perseverance set a new distance record on 11 October (45.22 km, past the 45.16 km that NASA's Opportunity rover drove), and on 24 October it drilled its first new rock sample in more than a year, "Singita", which NASA's team blog (posted 9 November) says may be among the oldest rocks in the rover's collection. Curiosity drilled a new hole at a block called "Nazca" on 20 October, its 49th by the team blog's count (NASA blog, posted 9 November; NASA's mission page still shows 42 holes). Japan's Martian Moons eXploration probe (MMX) launched on 20 October and is on its way; JAXA says its critical first days in space are done and the spacecraft is healthy; on 30 October the French space agency CNES woke the small Idefix rover riding on MMX for a planned test, which went well. Arrival at Mars is August 2027 per ESA, NASA and NASASpaceFlight; JAXA's press kit gives only "fiscal year 2027" (April 2027 to March 2028). NASA published (26 October) the first measurements on Mars of the very fine dust that future crews would have to deal with. NASA's four-person, yearlong Mars simulation on Earth (CHAPEA) ended on 31 October, when the crew left the pretend Mars base in Houston after 378 days; NASA says a follow-on program could start as soon as August 2027 [aspirational]. NASA's twin ESCAPADE orbiters are now on their way to Mars: each flew close past Earth and fired its engine for about 9 minutes, the first on 7 November and the second on 9 November, and NASA says both maneuvers went flawlessly (NASA, 9 November; UC Berkeley, which runs the mission, agrees). They reach Mars on 7 and 9 September 2027. On 9 November a space reporter, Irene Klotz of Aviation Week, reported from a meeting of Mars scientists that NASA will start a one-year study in January 2027 of how to bring Perseverance's samples to Earth [unconfirmed; no NASA page yet]. SpaceX itself now says Starship Flight 15, an Earth-orbit test that would try to catch both the booster and the ship, could launch as early as 13 November, pending regulatory approval (SpaceX mission page, 7 November); no FAA license is shown yet [aspirational until flown]. On 7 November NASA said JPL will build a nuclear-powered Moon rover, PROMISE, from spare parts and test models of the Curiosity and Perseverance Mars rovers, for launch in late 2028 [aspirational]. ESA marked ten years of its Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) at Mars on 19 October. New on 29 October: a NASA-funded study in the journal Science dates a meteorite from Mars found in the Sahara, "Teghaza 001", to more than 4.1 billion years ago, making it one of the oldest pieces of Mars known. New on 4 November: ESA's Trace Gas Orbiter has found hydrogen chloride gas coming from fresh cracks on the Alba Mons volcano, a possible sign that Mars still has warm magma underground (not proof of eruptions). NASA's review board report on the lost MAVEN orbiter blames a computer reboot followed by a faulty gyroscope.

Budget and Congress: a stopgap funding law keeps NASA at its 2026 level of $24.4 billion through 11 December 2026. The White House asked for $18.8 billion for 2027, and the House committee bill kept NASA flat at $24.4 billion. Mars Sample Return (bringing Perseverance's rock tubes to Earth) was cancelled and has no replacement plan; on 9 November Aviation Week's Irene Klotz reported that NASA will begin a one-year study of new ways to return the samples in January 2027 (a study, not a funded mission) [unconfirmed; no NASA page yet]. Two bid protests (formal challenges to a contract award) are now open at the Government Accountability Office (GAO) against NASA's Mars Telecommunications Network award to Blue Origin; the second was filed on 23 October. Democrats won both the House and the Senate in the 3 November elections and take over on 3 January 2027; the current Republican-led Congress, back at work on 9 November, still has to pass the 2027 spending bills or extend the stopgap past 11 December; the House plans to stop for the year on 17 December and the Senate on 18 December, dates that could change (SpacePolicyOnline, 8 November). A White House proclamation on 3 November speaks of Americans on Mars but sets no date or money.

Plans from companies and agencies are goals, not funded schedules, unless the entry says otherwise. They are marked [aspirational]. Facts I could not match to a second source are marked [unconfirmed]. A sol is one Martian day, about 24 hours 39 minutes.

whats_new.text: Both of NASA's ESCAPADE orbiters fired their engines while swinging past Earth, on 7 and 9 November, and are now on their way to Mars; NASA says both maneuvers went flawlessly. They are due to arrive on 7 and 9 September 2027.

NASA plans a one-year study, starting in January 2027, of new ways to bring Perseverance's rock samples to Earth, according to Aviation Week's Irene Klotz, reporting what NASA's Mars program head told a meeting of Mars scientists on 9 November. NASA has posted nothing on it yet [unconfirmed].

Curiosity has drilled a new hole in "Nazca", a rock block with what may be small crystals (20 October, per NASA's team blog posted 9 November). NASA's blog also now confirms Perseverance's "Singita" sample, its first in more than a year.

feed.text: Both ESCAPADE orbiters are now on their way to Mars, NASA says. Each flew close past Earth and fired its engine for about 9 minutes while Earth's gravity also sped it up and bent its path, a "powered flyby". The firing is the trans-Mars injection burn, the push that commits a spacecraft to its path to Mars. The first craft (Blue) finished at 5 AM U.S. Eastern on 7 November (noon Israel time), about 1,000 miles (about 1,600 km, our own conversion) above Earth; the second (Gold) at 6 AM Eastern on 9 November (1 PM Israel time), about 650 miles (about 1,050 km) up. NASA's Asal Naseri: "This is the first time NASA has used a powered Earth flyby to propel a spacecraft toward Mars, and we've now executed this maneuver twice, flawlessly, in just two days." Next come about 10 months of cruise with small course corrections, engine burns of about 11 minutes to enter Mars orbit on 7 and 9 September 2027, and science from June 2028.
feed.evidence: NASA's own story, matched by UC Berkeley's, which names Blue and Gold and calls it the first successful powered Earth gravity assist for a deep-space mission (Berkeley's claim). This settles the 7 November result that the news site Starlust reported early (item below). One difference: Berkeley says Blue enters Mars orbit on 9 September and Gold on 7 September, while NASA's 2 November blog gave 7 and 9 September for the first and second craft "respectively" [which craft arrives first is unconfirmed]. Berkeley's km figures (1,700 and 1,000 km) do not match its own miles; this page uses NASA's miles. No new picture: the run could not add image files, and NASA's new pictures are credited to Advanced Space and UC Berkeley.

feed.text: Curiosity has drilled "Nazca", the block with disc-shaped possible crystals that the team came back for. A Mastcam picture shows the new hole on sol 5050 (20 October; a sol is one Martian day, about 24 hours 39 minutes). Rock powder went to CheMin and SAM, the two labs inside the rover that identify minerals and chemicals; another drop to SAM, a drill clean-out and more pictures were still to come. The rover then took a few quiet sols to recharge its batteries, and on sol 5061 tested running two jobs at once (moving CheMin data while sending data to an orbiter) to save power, since its power output slowly falls as it ages.

feed.text: NASA's own blog now confirms the "Singita" sample. A hard rock called "Badger Peak" could not be cored, so the rover drove about 100 meters to similar light-toned rocks, ground a test patch called "Pumbe" (sol 2011, 17 October) and cored Singita on sol 2018 (24 October), its first sample in more than a year; the drill went about 3.1 cm into the rock. The rock is a gabbro (a coarse-grained rock that cooled from molten rock underground); the team thinks it formed deep in the crust and was dug up by one or more large impacts, so it may be among the oldest rocks collected. It was the rover's 66th abrasion (a small patch ground flat to see inside a rock). Separately, SuperCam keeps finding tiny grains of corundum with chromium, the mineral that makes ruby; on Mars it probably points to heating by large impacts, not gems.
feed.evidence: NASA team blogs; they match the Planetary Society's 28 October report (item below), which now rests on NASA too. The corundum result was published earlier this year in Geophysical Research Letters by a team led by Ann Ollila (per the blog; the paper was not opened). The blog says the latest status report calls the rover "healthy and stable".

feed.text: At an event at NASA's Kennedy Space Center on Saturday, 7 November, NASA announced a set of Moon Base awards. One reuses Mars hardware: NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) will build PROMISE (Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration), a six-wheeled, nuclear-powered rover for the Moon's South Pole, "from a combination of spare flight components and engineering test models for NASA's Curiosity and Perseverance Mars rovers". NASA says this cuts cost and time. PROMISE would drill about 1 meter (3 feet) down to look for ice. NASA is targeting late 2028 for launch and an 18-month mission [aspirational]; Blue Origin gets a $94 million base contract, with a $140 million option, to land it with its Mark 1 lander. The release also says NASA's Moon presence will "build on this foundation for the first crewed mission to Mars", with no Mars date. The same day NASA opened applications for a new astronaut class, which it says will "lay the groundwork for the first crewed missions to Mars" (no date either).
feed.evidence: NASA's own release and mission page (an interested source on its own plans). SpaceNews's headline (7 November) agrees that NASA will convert a Mars rover engineering model into a lunar rover for 2028; the rest of its story is behind a sign-up wall. Which Curiosity or Perseverance parts are used is not listed [unconfirmed]. A second award in the release has SpaceX launch communications satellites on a Starship to the area around the Moon in 2028 [aspirational].

Starlust reports that it "successfully completed a powered fly-by of Earth and is now headed towards Mars", "according to NASA". The second orbiter ("Gold") burns at 5:51 AM Eastern on 9 November (12:51 PM Israel time). NASA said earlier that the team will know how well each craft is aimed for Mars only several days after the burns, and will correct the paths on the way.

feed.text: SpaceX now gives the date itself: Starship Flight 15 "is preparing to launch as soon as Friday, November 13, pending regulatory approval". The 75-minute window opens at 4:45 PM U.S. Central time (00:45 Israel time on 14 November, our own conversion). It would be the first flight to bring both the Super Heavy booster and the Starship upper stage back to the launch tower to be caught; SpaceX calls this a possible "first full recovery of an orbital launch system". The ship would fly about 14 times around Earth at about 275 km for more than 22 hours and release 26 Starlink V3 internet satellites. It returns to the launch site only if its systems are healthy; otherwise it can come down over the ocean. This is an Earth-orbit test, not a Mars flight; SpaceX still says Mars cargo flights start no earlier than 2028 [aspirational].

feed.text: ESA's Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) has found what ESA's blog calls "signs of young volcanism on present-day Mars". Its Atmospheric Chemistry Suite (ACS) instrument keeps detecting hydrogen chloride (HCl), a gas that comes out of volcanic vents on Earth, at about two parts per billion. The study traces it to the northern flanks of Alba Mons, a huge, low volcano, where TGO's CaSSIS camera saw fresh cracks and white spots that may be deposits around vents (an area about 20 by 20 km near 64.6°N, 274.4°E, imaged 3 February 2023). The gas shows up mostly in early northern summer; the team thinks ice and frozen ground hold it in during winter. The finding suggests magma may still be warm under Mars, but it is not proof of an eruption: no lava flow or eruption has ever been seen on Mars. Mège says hot-water systems underground could exist but would not have to host life. TGO's project scientist Colin Wilson told NASASpaceFlight the findings "may prove to be TGO's greatest success yet".

feed.where: science.nasa.gov (posted 2:11 PM U.S. Eastern time on 2 November; first seen in our 3 November check)
feed.text: NASA now gives the dates and times itself. Each of the two ESCAPADE orbiters will fly close past Earth and fire its engine at the closest point, a "powered flyby" (using Earth's gravity and an engine burn together, also called an Oberth maneuver), which NASA says no Mars-bound spacecraft has done successfully before. The first orbiter's burn begins at 4:51 AM U.S. Eastern time on Saturday 7 November (11:51 AM Israel time, our own conversion); the second at 5:51 AM Eastern on Monday 9 November (12:51 PM Israel time). Each "trans-Mars injection burn" (the push that sends a craft from Earth toward Mars) lasts about 9 minutes and raises its speed from about 6.3 to about 6.7 miles per second (about 10.1 to 10.8 km per second, our own arithmetic). At closest approach the orbiters will be 600 to 1,100 miles (about 970 to 1,770 km) above the ground. After a 10-month cruise they reach Mars on 7 and 9 September 2027. NASA adds that during the year-long loop near Earth the pair flew through a distant part of Earth's magnetotail (the part of Earth's magnetic field stretched out behind it by the solar wind) that no spacecraft had sampled directly, with results to come. Skywatchers with telescopes may see them as faint moving dots: from the western U.S. in the hours before each burn, and from southern Australia during the burns.

feed.who: NASA's MAVEN Anomaly Review Board report (dated 17 July 2026), reported by SpaceNews (Jeff Foust)
feed.kind: official (NASA/JPL report) and a news report
feed.where: assets.science.nasa.gov (PDF); spacenews.com (2 November, 19:12 Israel time; first seen in our 5 November check)
feed.text: NASA's review board says the MAVEN orbiter, lost on 6 December 2025, most likely died from an unrequested reboot of its flight computer, caused either by a radiation hit (a "single-event upset") or a software problem. The reboot switched on its worn-out gyroscope unit (the sensor that tracks rotation), which gave false readings, so the spacecraft spun itself up to about 2.3 to 2.7 turns per minute and could not recover; its last signal came about 4 hours 20 minutes after the problem began. The board could not prove a single cause because little data came back. It says MAVEN is probably intact in a stable orbit and is no debris risk to other Mars orbiters. It recommends that all Mars orbiters have a robust way to fly without gyroscopes and better fault protection. MAVEN had worked at Mars for over 11 years, 8 beyond its design.
feed.evidence: Read in the board's report itself (36 pages, chaired by Hoppy Price of JPL). SpaceNews's summary ("a computer glitch and a faulty gyro") matches; the rest of its story is behind a sign-up wall. The report is dated 17 July; when NASA posted it is not stated [unconfirmed].

feed.text: The four CHAPEA volunteers came out of NASA's pretend Mars base at Johnson Space Center in Houston on Saturday, 31 October, after 378 days inside. The crew had been inside since 19 October 2025: Ross Elder (commander), Ellen Ellis (medical officer), Matthew Montgomery (science officer) and James Spicer (flight engineer). Johnson's director, Vanessa Wyche, said messages to the crew were delayed 26 to 44 minutes each way, as they would be from Mars. Suzanne Bell, a researcher on the study, said the crew also spent two weeks with no contact at all, to copy the time when the Sun blocks signals between Earth and Mars; the next two weeks are tests and debriefs. Elder called humans on Mars "not only achievable, but rather inevitable". NASA plans to fold CHAPEA into a new program, the Moon and Mars Exploration Analog, which could start as soon as August 2027 (Engadget, Mariella Moon, 31 October, says no earlier than August 2027 and that applications are open) [aspirational].

feed.who: NASA, news release 2026-079, "NASA-funded Study Details One of Oldest Mars Meteorites Ever Found"
feed.where: nasa.gov (posted 2:18 p.m. U.S. Eastern time, 20:18 Israel time)
feed.text: A rose-colored meteorite (a rock that fell to Earth from space) found in the Sahara in Mali in 2022, named Teghaza 001, formed on Mars more than 4.1 billion years ago, according to a study published 29 October in the journal Science. That makes it one of the three oldest of the roughly 435 Martian meteorites known; the others are ALH84001, found in Antarctica in 1984, which is of similar age, and "Black Beauty". Water altered the rock about 4.1 billion years ago, so it formed even earlier, and the team says this supports the idea that early Mars had liquid water and conditions that could have suited life, though it does not show that life existed. It is a single kind of coarse igneous rock (gabbro, which cooled slowly from molten rock below the surface), unlike Black Beauty, which is a jumble of many rock pieces. Its minerals best match Mars's ancient southern highlands as seen from orbit by NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO); NASA shows 13 possible source spots on a MOLA map (an elevation map made by a laser altimeter on the old Mars Global Surveyor orbiter). The lead author is Yang Liu of JPL; the University of New Mexico first spotted that it came from Mars from its oxygen isotopes (different forms of the oxygen atom).
feed.evidence: official NASA release about a peer-reviewed paper; the main facts (found in Mali in 2022, at least 4.1 billion years old, about 435 Martian meteorites, lead author Liu) match Reuters (Will Dunham, 29 Oct) and the University of New Mexico's own release. I did not open the Science paper itself (the journal site refused my reader)
feed.other: The sources describe the dating a little differently: NASA names rubidium-strontium dating of mineral grains, while Reuters and the University of New Mexico describe uranium-lead dating of tiny zircon crystals; the paper may use both [unconfirmed]. Reuters reports the rock was found in eight pieces about 34 km (21 miles) from the village of Bir Chali, and quotes Liu that it may come from near the Hellas Basin, a huge impact crater. NASA puts it at about 800 grams (nearly 2 pounds); Space.com (Samantha Mathewson, 6 November) gives the same 800 grams. The University of New Mexico is a partner in the study (an interested source). @NASAMars posted the story on X at 22:10 Israel time.

feed.text: For the first time in more than a year, Perseverance has collected a rock sample. On 24 October it drilled a core called "Singita" in the "Lac de Charmes" region outside the western rim of Jezero crater. The news was first given by Katie Stack Morgan, the mission's project scientist, at the American Astronomical Society's planetary sciences meeting (the Division for Planetary Sciences, DPS). Only lab work on Earth could give its exact age. The rock was so hard that the first try failed, and the rover switched to a less-used drill bit. feed.text: Over 1,645 sols (Martian days), Perseverance measured how much very fine dust settled on small squares of spacesuit material it carries: Teflon and Vectran (a strong woven fiber) on the calibration target of its SHERLOC instrument (an ultraviolet scanner that looks for minerals and carbon compounds), and Teflon and basalt glass on the target of PIXL (an X-ray instrument that reads the chemistry of rocks). It is the first measurement on Mars itself of fine dust (smaller than 2.5 micrometers, far thinner than a hair) and ultrafine dust (about 100 nanometers). Grains averaged about 2 micrometers on some swatches and only 100 to 300 nanometers on others; static electricity decides which grains stick to which material. The dust is rich in iron and sulfur, has extra phosphorus and signs of calcium sulfate, and Mars dust also carries perchlorates (salts that are toxic to people). The study, led by Scott VanBommel of Washington University in St. Louis, was published on 27 October in PNAS (Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences). Quoted: Lindsay Hays, acting director of NASA's Planetary Science Division, and Katie Stack Morgan, the project scientist at JPL.

feed.who: ESA, "A Mars-velous decade: Celebrating ten years of TGO" (ESA operations news)
feed.where: esa.int (dated 19 October; first seen in our 4 November check, in ESA's operations news feed, which earlier checks did not read)
feed.text: ESA marked ten years since its ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) reached Mars on 19 October 2016 at 15:24 UTC. The same day its small Schiaparelli lander was lost because a software problem shut its descent engines off too early; ESA says the lessons were applied to the Rosalind Franklin rover. From about 400 km up, TGO studies trace gases (gases present in tiny amounts). It has not detected methane, despite earlier reports of methane on Mars by other missions; it made the first detection of hydrogen chloride in Mars's air; it has measured water loss; its camera has mapped more than 10% of the surface in four colors, partly to study landing sites for Rosalind Franklin; and it has monitored radiation and mapped ice under the ground. It is also a relay for messages between Earth and the surface. Flight software sent up in 2024 limits use of its gyroscopes (the sensors that track which way it points) to save them for Rosalind Franklin's arrival. TGO can now store data from the surface during solar conjunction (when the Sun sits between Earth and Mars and blocks contact) and send it later. Its surface radio is now also used with Mars Express to study the atmosphere. The story gives no end date for the mission.
feed.evidence: ESA's own story, quoting Silvia Sangiorgi (head of ESA's Mars mission operations unit), Colin Wilson (TGO project scientist), Peter Schmitz (spacecraft operations manager) and Jorge Vago (ExoMars project scientist). The 19 October 2016 arrival matches ESA's TGO facts-and-figures page of 15 October.

feed.text: Before ESA's Rosalind Franklin rover can explore Mars it must drive off its landing platform, which ESA calls one of the mission's most critical moments. In a two-month test in Turin, Italy, a full-size twin rover called Amalia drove off a model of the platform more than 20 times: with a ceiling hoist carrying two-thirds of its weight to copy Mars's lower gravity, on a platform tilted 20 degrees, and with obstacles under the ramps. The platform has two pairs of ramps, front and back, and ground control will choose which way to drive off using only pictures from orbit; "once we egress, there is no way back," said Eric Zekri, ESA's ExoMars rover team leader. The rover weighs 300 kg on Earth; the 3-meter aluminum ramps were made by the Polish company Astronika, and the tests were run by Thales Alenia Space (the main contractor) at ALTEC. ESA says the rover's journey on the Martian surface begins in 2030.

board.s: Working. Drilled "Nazca", a block with possible crystal shapes, on sol 5050 (20 Oct); the team blog calls it the 49th drill hole, while NASA's mission page still shows 42 [the two NASA counts disagree; unconfirmed]. Powder went to the CheMin and SAM labs; the rover then rested to recharge (NASA blogs, posted 9 Nov). Before that it finished drilling at Basque Lakes. Climbing Mount Sharp; 1 km of elevation gain reached 26 Aug 2026. FY2027 request keeps it funded at $38.0M. NASA's raw-image feed now shows pictures through sol 5069 (9 Nov), including Navcam frames with a new drive number, a hint that it moved [our own reading]. On 7 Nov NASA said spare parts and test models from Curiosity and Perseverance will be used to build PROMISE, a Moon rover.

board.s: Working. World-record 45.22 km driven by sol 2006 (11 Oct); NASA's traverse file shows 45.25 km by sol 2022 (28 Oct). Exploring Lac de Charmes, outside Jezero's western rim, near the Idubi outcrop. Drilled a new sample, "Singita", on sol 2018 (24 Oct), its first in more than a year, about 3.1 cm into a gabbro that may be among its oldest rocks; now confirmed by NASA's team blog (posted 9 Nov), first reported by the Planetary Society. 66 abrasions so far; SuperCam finds tiny corundum (ruby-mineral) grains, likely from impact heating. NASA counted 29 rock and regolith samples before that, none returned; first mission extension began in October, to about end of 2028. FY2027 request would cut operations from $87.5M (2024) to $38.0M. New on 26 Oct: NASA published its dust study from swatches of spacesuit material the rover carries.

board.s: Launched 13 Nov 2025 on Blue Origin's New Glenn. The Mars departure burn is in November 2026 and arrival is September 2027 per the Berkeley mission-design page. NASA's ESCAPADE blog (2 Nov) gives the powered Earth flybys and engine burns on 7 November (first orbiter, burn at 4:51 AM U.S. Eastern) and 9 November (second, 5:51 AM Eastern), matching Eos (27 Oct, Blue then Gold), and arrival on 7 and 9 September 2027. Result: both burns worked. NASA (9 Nov) says the first craft finished its burn at 5 AM Eastern on 7 Nov, about 1,000 miles up, and the second at 6 AM Eastern on 9 Nov, about 650 miles up (Berkeley names them Blue and Gold), "flawlessly"; UC Berkeley agrees. Both are now cruising to Mars, with course corrections on the way and science from June 2028. Berkeley says Blue arrives 9 Sep and Gold 7 Sep, the reverse of NASA's earlier order [unconfirmed]. The news site Starlust had reported the first success early. Rocket Lab, the builder, gave the same burn dates on X (3 Nov). Advanced Space, which designs the path, says Blue passes Earth on the night of 6 Nov (U.S. time) and Gold about 49 hours later, and that binoculars may show them (X, 5 Nov). Each orbiter weighs 535 kg fueled, 209 kg dry (NASA mission page). FY2027 request: $4.5M.

curiosity.t: Latest NASA blogs, both posted 9 November 2026: sols 5050 to 5055 (Susanne P. Schwenzer, The Open University, plan of 23 October) says the rover "successfully drilled our 49th drill hole, called 'Nazca'"; a Mastcam picture of the hole is dated sol 5050 (20 October). Powder went to the CheMin lab, and the rover also zapped dark pebbles with ChemCam's laser. Sols 5056 to 5062 (Remington Free, NASA JPL, plan of 30 October): samples dropped to SAM and CheMin, a few sols of rest to recharge, and a first test of running two power-hungry jobs at once to save energy. NASA's mission page still shows 42 drill holes, so the count is unsettled [unconfirmed].

Earlier NASA blog: sols 5043 to 5049, posted 28 October 2026 by Lucy Lim (NASA Goddard). After Basque Lakes the rover went back near "Chiu Chiu" and is preparing to drill "Nazca", a block packed with disc- and needle-shaped possible crystals. It also planned night pictures of Phobos to study high, thin clouds; the twilight cloud season is starting. The plan was from 16 October; the drilling came on sol 5050.
The previous blog (sols 5036 to 5042, 19 October, Alex Innanen): drill campaign at "Basque Lakes" finished; it is autumn in Gale crater; a new Mars year (number 39) began at the end of September.

NASA's raw-image feed has pictures through sol 5069, taken on 9 November 2026: MAHLI close-ups, ChemCam, hazard cameras and 66 Navcam frames whose file names carry a new drive number (1252082, up from 1251326 on sol 5068), a hint that the rover moved [our own reading of the file names, unconfirmed]. Sol 5068 also has seven Mastcam frames. So 10 November is about sol 5070 (our own arithmetic). The picture above is still the sol 5062 Navcam view (2 November): this run could not add new picture files, so the sol 5069 Navcam view is linked instead. NASA's pages that I opened give no odometer for these sols, so none is shown here.

Climbing Mount Sharp, the mound in Gale crater: 1 kilometer of elevation gain reached on 26 August 2026, per NASA's mission page, which still counts 42 drill holes (checked 10 November; the 9 November blog says 49).

Distance: NASA's 12 October record release says Curiosity has driven more than 38.07 km (23.65 miles). Money: the FY2027 request puts Curiosity (the Mars Science Laboratory line) at $38.0M, from $40.0M in the 2024 plan (AAS summary of NASA's request); Congress has not set the final 2027 number.

plans.t: No agency has an approved, funded, dated crewed mission to Mars as of 8 November 2026 that I could find. NASA's 7 November call for new astronauts says the class will "lay the groundwork for the first crewed missions to Mars", again with no date. NASA calls Mars a "horizon goal" after the Moon (course, citing NASA release 26-025, which I did not open). glossary: Sol
one Martian day, about 24 hours 39 minutes. Rovers count their days in sols from landing.
MOLA
the Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter, an instrument that measured Mars's heights by laser; used for the course's maps.
ISRU
in-situ resource use: making water, air or fuel from what is already on Mars instead of bringing it.
GAO bid protest
a company challenges a federal contract award at the Government Accountability Office, which must decide within about 100 days.
CR
continuing resolution: a stopgap law that keeps agencies funded at last year's level while Congress finishes the new budget.
Fiscal year (Japan)
Japan's government year runs from April to March, so "fiscal year 2027" means April 2027 to March 2028.
HCl
hydrogen chloride, a sharp-smelling gas; on Earth it comes out of volcanic vents. Measured on Mars in parts per billion (ppb), billionths of the air.
Anomaly Review Board
a NASA panel that investigates why a spacecraft failed and recommends fixes for future missions.
MEPAG
the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group, NASA's forum where Mars scientists hear NASA's plans and give advice.
Abrasion
grinding a small patch of rock flat (about 5 cm across on Perseverance) to see its fresh inside before deciding whether to sample it.
Trans-Mars injection
the engine firing that sends a spacecraft out of Earth's neighborhood onto its path to Mars.
Mars window
the roughly 26-month period when Earth and Mars line up well for a launch.
